div1.p:
The following oral history is the result of an
audiotaped interview with Mr. William R. Willert on
July 21, 2001, conducted by Tom Swope. The interview
took place in Euclid, Ohio, and is part of the Library
of Congress collection of oral testimonies.

This interview was transcribed and processed by
Vivian Baumhover, CSR, RPR, of Des Moines, Iowa, in
March of 2003.

The reader should bear in mind that she or he is
reading a verbatim transcript of spoken rather than
written prose. Insofar as possible, this transcript
tries to represent the spoken word. Thus, it should be
read as a personal memoir and not as either a
researched monograph or edited account.

To the extent possible, the spelling of place
names, foreign words, and personal names have been
verified, either by reference resources or directly
by the interviewee. Some uncertainties will inevitably
remain regarding some words and their spellings. In
these scenarios, a (ph) follows a word or name that is
spelled phonetically.

sp.speaker: TOM SWOPE:
sp.p:
This is the oral history of World War II veteran William R. Willert. Mr. Willertwas in
the U.S. Navy and served aboard the aircraft carrier
U.S.S. Belleau Wood. was a pilot of a TBM
Avenger and served in the Pacific. His highest rank
was Lieutenant JG. I'm Tom Swope, and we recorded this
at Mr. Willert's home in Euclid, Ohio, on July 21st,
2001. Bill's age at the time was 80.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Question. So when did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
Answer: Well, I was going to Fenn College. I
started there in '30 -- late '39, and I -- there were
quarterly programs because Fenn was a co-op college,
something I could afford, about $300 a quarter. But I
was going -- I -- first thing I did was to go down
there to find out how -- what I needed, and I started
probably in the latter part of '39. I can't recall the
month. And then I stayed there from '39 and '40. And,
of course, in '41 it hit the fan, and I immediately
tried to find out -- listening to my dad about World
War I in France fighting in the trenches kind of
discouraged me of playing in the mud, so I thought,
"Dad, if it's all right with you, I'm going to join
the Navy." I don't know what caused me to do that, but
I had to go downtown to Cleveland to find out a little bit about the Navy because I wanted to become a pilot,
and I don't know why that either. But they said I
would have to go to Columbus to enlist. They didn't
know how to do it here. So I borrowed my dad's car and
drove down to Columbus, and I passed all the tests, but
they didn't sign me up. And about two or three months
later I'm sitting there waiting for something, and
suddenly I got a draft notice, and that really scared
me. I said, "I don't want any part of it." So I wrote
them a quick letter, and it was the kind you sign for
because I wanted to make sure the right people got it.
Anyway, they said, "Go ahead and take the test and then
come down here." And so I drove -- you can tell, I
drove 150 miles one way twice just to get into the
service. I didn't drive a thousand miles north to get
out of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Right.

sp.speaker: William R. Willert
sp.p:
A. Anyhow, they finally signed me up. And then I
got a list here of all the things that I went through.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Getting back to Pearl Harbor, do you remember
specifically where you were when Pearl Harbor was --

sp.speaker: William R. Willert
sp.p:
A. Yes, I was in school, definitely at Fenn
College. And I knew right away that this was going to
be trouble, but I didn't know how. I wanted to get
involved, like I said. My dad was -- he was kind of a nervous wreck, and I had an uncle who was in World
War I also, and he ended up in Chillicothe Veterans
Hospital, where -- some kind of a head case that ends
up down there. But when I enlisted, after they finally
signed me up, they told me I was going to go to Detroit
for some indoctrination, and so I went. And then they
gave me a choice -- that was nice. They gave me a
choice -- a piece of paper that had colleges on. They
said, "If you want to get in the V5 program, here's a
list of colleges that you can pick." So they had
Baldwin Wallace, they had Case, they had Western
Reserve, and they had Fenn. So I put down all four of
them because -- Fenn was first. So I came back, and
Fenn sent me of all places to Borea to learn the
basics, and how to fly was done at Cleveland Hopkins
Airport, but it wasn't Cleveland Hopkins then. It was
just a big mat, no runways. The biggest plane I think
they had ever landed there at the time was probably a
DC-3. But anyway, they got -- they had the Aroncas,
which is a two-seating plane, with an instructor and a
pilot or somebody that was hoping to be a pilot, and
they taught us how to fly. And this was in the winter
of probably '42, and we usually had no problem. There
were no radio in the car -- in the plane. So when you
took off, you had to watch the lights in the tower. A yellow light means okay, and green light meant land,
red light, don't land. So we -- all we did was fly
around the field just to get the feel of the plane and
how to taxi and how to take off and how to land. That
was -- the main -- the main thing in flying was how to
land because if you can walk away from it, it's a good
one. So we did that for three months, and there
were -- there were about maybe a dozen V5 fellas there
and maybe another dozen or two fellas that were
learning to fly for the Army, mostly to learn how to
transport aircraft from one base to another. That
certainly wasn't my idea of fighting a war, but that's
what they wanted to do. And there were a lot of
courses I had to take there, but I finally graduated.
And then they sent me home on leave. And it took -- I
could take a streetcar home from the old airport
because it used to run right up to the front, and it
took two and a half hours to get from the airport to
Cleveland Heights. I had to take the streetcar to the
public square, get on another streetcar and take me up
to Noble and Mayfield, and then I would get on a bus,
and that would take me down to where -- near where I
lived. That was an interesting trip. I didn't do it
too often.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. What did the V5 designation, what did that mean?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
V5. Well, V in the Navy means heavier than
air, and 5 was just the group --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Okay.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. -- that they were -- because they had all kinds
of Vs. But anytime you see a V in the Navy, it means
heavier than air because if you flew in a blimp, it
wouldn't be a V.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Okay.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. It would -- or -- no matter what kind of a --
if the plane was heavier than air, it had -- it was a V
program.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. So whenever you see a VMF or whatever, a V
designation on a squadron --

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. Right, right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. -- that's what that means?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. All the letters have like a V -- my air group
was Air Group 30. Now, the fighters were called VF and
the torpedo -- the bombers -- well, actually the
torpedo squadron was VT, and then it's a number,
because there's all kinds of torpedo squadrons. So the
T designated the -- and the same way with aircraft.
They all had different ways of designating, like the
Avenger, the original was built by Grumman, and that's
called a TBF. And torpedo bomber, F stood for Grumman. And later on Grumman got too busy making
fighter planes, the F-6 Hellcat, and so they farmed it
out to General Motors. So that's why the plane became
a TBM. But they make good planes. I mean, they were
all -- I had no problem with my first TBM. After I
finished at Fenn, I think they sent me down to
Chapel Hill, North Carolina, at the University of North
Carolina. And we stayed there, and they call that
learning but no flying. And I'm telling you, we had to
run the obstacle course every morning first thing.
They fed us well, but everything was called rough,
tough and smart down there. We did nothing but -- we
did track which was not rough, and we did soccer and
that was rough. And I recall one -- the only soccer
game that I ever played in, two students met each other
head on. One of them got up and the other was carried
away. I don't know whether -- I think he broke a leg,
but I didn't follow up on that. But anyway, the Navy
built a huge swimming pool down there, and we spent at
least four hours a day in that swimming pool, not only
learning to swim but how to save yourself if you ever
got shot down. We had to learn how to turn our shirt
into a Mae West or some kind of a air holder, and we
also had to do that with our pants. We had khaki pants
back then. And then they would put us in a makeshift cockpit, and we'd go on a hill and right into the pool,
and you had to learn how to get out of there. Of
course, if you land a Grumman Avenger in the water, you
don't have any bottom to that pool. I think it would
float for about 30 seconds if you landed it properly.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. And that was my deal after we all got together,
my crew and myself, I said, "Look, if I'm able, I'm
going to land the thing, and you two guys get the
four-man life raft out." And there's a big bag of
goodies that we filled up with things that we wanted in
case we were going to be floating for a week or two.
And I keep telling people, I says, "It's the only time
I ever used the condom." I said, "The skipper -- the
flight surgeon would give us these things, and we would
wrap our cigarettes in them so that we didn't want them
to get wet." I said, "That's the only time I used
them."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Makes sense

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Yeah. And the trouble is aboard ship during a
typhoon, the -- some little truck got loose on the
hanger deck and tore the tail off my plane, and they
just threw the thing overboard. The only thing I got
out of it is a clock. That's upstairs by itself.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Did you keep a lot of your personal -- some of your personal things on the plane?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Well, no, just in the -- just -- no, just the
things that we needed for the flight.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh, right.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. We did -- we weren't allowed to fly -- or smoke
on takeoff, but as soon as we were in the air, it was
up to us. But normally when you're flying with an air
group of five or six other planes, you're flying so
close to them that you ain't got time to diddle around
with CDs and tapes and all this other stuff that they
got nowadays. Matter of fact, we had -- if we were
going on a mission, we were loaded with up to 2,000
pounds of bombs or one torpedo. And that's another
thing, we took turns to drop those. If it were
bombs -- 500-pound bombs, we had four of them. The
original Avenger was designed to drop a torpedo at
about 50 feet, and they found out -- the Torpedo
Squadron 8 didn't have the Avenger. They were flying
another aircraft, and they had -- the torpedoes were
rotten then, absolutely rotten. They didn't shoot --
even if they were -- would survive the attack, they
weren't sure if the torpedo would explode, and a lot of
them didn't. And that's why when you're flying at 50
feet, the enemy guns, all they had to do was fire a
shell into the water and the explosion would throw water up and that would knock the plane down, and they
did that. I met Ensign Gabe (ph) at one of our
reunions down in Charleston, South Carolina. He has
since died. But I've read the stories and heard the
stories about what he had to go through, and he ended
up getting shot down too, but he was the only
survivor. And I didn't realize at the time that he
didn't have an Avenger. I thought he did, but he
didn't. His was a different aircraft, and I can't
recall the type at the time, but he ended up sitting in
the water in his -- well, his Mae West. They finally
picked him up after they dispersed the enemies, but
that's why they all got shot down. The torpedoes were
no good. They had to drop them at 50 feet. And later
on in my experience on the carrier, only once did we
carry a torpedo out of 26 flights that I made, as I
started to say before I spilled the beans.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. What was the exact name of your unit?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. VT 30. It was called Torpedo Squadron 30. I
will give you some history of that because that -- it
started prior to my getting into it. Our -- the group
that I was with, it seemed like it took so damn long to
get into action. I didn't think I was going to make
the war because I enlisted in '42 June. I was sworn in
in August of '42, and I didn't even get aboard the carrier until 19 -- January of '45. And I went -- you
know, I spent a lot of time learning.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. So you did not go overseas until 1945 then?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Correct, yeah. Here's a chronology of what I
did. But after I left Chapel Hill we came home -- and
here again, I learned this later, but the Navy for some
reason was a big drawing card back then. They had
pilots coming out of their ears or prospective pilots,
and they had to delay them. Now, George Bush was one
of them, and he cheated and got in. He was the
youngest Navy pilot ever to get in, and I think there
was a guy in my group that was the second youngest.
But that's a debate. But anyway, every time we went to
a base, we were sent home for two weeks and then sent
to another base. After Chapel Hill I was sent to a
little town in Indiana called Bunker Hill. That later
ended up as a Air Force base, and I mean Air Force, not
Army Air Corps. The Air Force is about 51 years old
now, I think. Anyhow, they took over the field after
the war. But anyway, in Bunker Hill we learned how to
fly the Stearman that we saw out at the -- and that's
what they were giving rides in. It's a two-seater.
Yellow Peril they called it. It was built by Stearman
back then. Now it's owned by Boeing, and I didn't know
that until the other day. This was -- this is a good
aircraft. If they had had a dozen of these in World
War I, they could have won that war six months earlier
because that plane was not like those things that the
Germans and the French and whoever -- I'm not too sure
what they did over there, but I know about the Red
Baron and all that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Right.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. But that Stearman was a -- we would go up there
with an instructor for several weeks and just fly
around. Indiana is flat country. All you did was look
for the Wabash River and the only place you would see
any trees. We never flew over any cities because they
were -- or towns. There was strict rules about that,
and the altitude rules are still pretty high. The only
time you're low is when you land. But anyway, we would
fly around there, and the Stearman -- the instructor
would take you up, and he would control the plane for a
while, and then suddenly he would cut the engine. He
would say, "Okay. Land it." And this is how we learned
because you never know when you're ready to do this.
You have to be prepared for these things, and he did it
well. But we actually would touch those wheels to the
ground and then ________+ the old throttle. I'm not
sure whether there was a throttle in both cockpits. I
think only one. So if he cut it, you couldn't correct it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. But anyway, we would do that for -- that took
another three months. Sent me home on leave again.
And -- well, Bunker Hill was, I think, the last place
until I was sent to I think it says Pensacola next.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Pensacola, right. October of '43 Pensacola
Naval Air Station.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. And that one I stayed at for nine months. I
didn't think I'd ever get the heck out of there. And
back in those days Pensacola had nine airfields. Each
one was designated for different types of learning
things, and we would try them all because they didn't
know at the time, and neither did we, whether you were
going to be a fighter pilot or torpedo pilot,
amphibious pilot or whatever. And you had to learn all
the tricks of the trade. And down there we -- on that
program that we had at the museum, there was the
Valty (ph) vibrator they called it, which was a fixed
landing gear type of plane, but it was a two-seater.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. And you learned in that first. Then they
finally gave us the SNJ which had a retractable landing
gear, and it also had two .30 caliber machine guns, one
on each wing. And that was for further training, and
INTERVIEW WITH WILLIAM R. WILLERT 7-21-01 15
we would fly for maybe a half an hour or so. And they
would paint each of our bullets a different color, and
another plane would tow what they called a sleeve. It
was probably about two or three feet in diameter and
just nothing, air in it. And we would take turns
strafing that. And, in fact, later on I think even our
crew -- I didn't have a crew right away, but later on
when I did, they were able to fire another gun in a
specially built plane for that. But anyway, I wanted
to be -- everybody wants to be a fighter pilot, but
they not only trained us how to strafe, they would --
they trained us how to drop little -- well, eventually
would be depth charges, but they were just two little
bombs that would leave a -- some kind of a mark on the
ocean. And this was -- the so-called submarine was a
flat board or something being towed by a boat, and we
would drop these special bombs. And if you were -- I
always got a hundred percent on that sucker. I still
have some of the pictures showing my -- the results.
And that's why I ended up with a torpedo instead of a
fighter. I was disappointed, but what the heck. And I
ended up with probably the easiest, the slowest and the
biggest single-engine plane in the Navy or in the world
for that matter. We could fly, oh, I think, like 200,
250 miles per hour on the level, but normally we'd fly
INTERVIEW WITH WILLIAM R. WILLERT 7-21-01 16
probably less than that, depending on the situation.
Okay. We would -- after we we learned all this stuff,
it took nine months. Matter of fact, we even had snow
while we were down there, and the southern pilots
didn't know what to do with it, so we showed them. We
went over to some of the aircraft and scraped up the
snow -- there wasn't much -- and we showed them how
to make snowballs. And we had a little fun doing
that. In fact, it was such a rarity that -- we learned
later that everybody in school and the local businesses
all came outside to see what it was like because they
never saw it before. I said, "Heck, I just come off of
the ice skating rinks in Cleveland," because I played
hockey here. I was playing hockey in high school when
I graduated, and I ended up playing hockey in the
amateur league and later on college. But no ice
skating in the Navy, so I just stopped playing hockey,
and I kept all my teeth too. Not now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. How big was the crew on the Avenger?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Well, the pilot, the gunner and a radio man.
The original idea was to put -- they had a -- the
original TBF had a .30 caliber machine gun firing down
and the .50 caliber firing up and sideways either way.
And by the time I got out there, they decided that .30
caliber was like throwing rice at a bride, so they got
INTERVIEW WITH WILLIAM R. WILLERT 7-21-01 17
rid of it and they put a camera in. It was -- and then
they gave that particular crewman a radio and a radar
machine down there, and he could use the radar to find
out where we were, you know, coming to anything or --
and, of course, he didn't use the radio unless I let
him because that was -- the Navy is very strict. You
don't fly and talk to people unless it's absolutely
necessary. But he would take pictures of whatever I
bombed. And I'm not sure he got a picture, but the day
I took -- I had my torpedo -- which I mentioned, our
carrier was so small that we only had enough for one
mission, and we got wind of a seven or eight group of
Jap ships that was in the South China Sea, so they sent
us up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Was this shortly after you got there then in
January of '45?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. No. That's when we left.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. We didn't -- that's another story.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Oh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. When we left the States in January, we went
under the Golden Gate Bridge and waved good-bye to the
U.S.A. and floated over to Hawaii, and we stopped there
for a day or two or three. I can't recall the length.
It might tell you in that group there. But anyway, we
went over with some very rare ships. They only made
one what they call battle cruiser and it was named the
Alaska, and I don't think you'll see that anywhere on
the -- well, there might be something. The Navy built
the thing, so they'll stick with it. The different
ships that we were with is in there somewhere. Bunker
Hill was there, and incidentally, the Bunker Hill has
got a connection too because the father of the current
Euclid mayor was on board that one. And that baby,
that carrier, really got hit by kamikazes later on in
the war. The Belleau Wood did too but prior to me
being on it. Fortunately I didn't get on it until
January of '45, but in October of '44 it got hit too on
the tail, and it killed a lot of people. I have a
picture of that upstairs, and I'll show you. But
anyway, when we -- all the way over we had the air
combat officer, ACI, Air Combat Intelligence,
explaining what our first mission was going to be, but
they didn't tell me or us where. We floated all the
way over there. I went ashore on -- at -- in Hawaii.
We were allowed to stay overnight one night, so we went
to the Ala Moana Hotel which was one of two at the
time, the Ala Moana and the Pink Palace, which are
still there. And we just wandered around and took
pictures, and some of us were able to keep the pictures, but come the -- in fact, I have some of those
pictures available somewhere. Anyway, we saw Waikiki
Beach. And the Pink Palace only had women nurses in
it, nothing else, so that's why we went to the
Ala Moana. We weren't allowed near -- for some reason
there was some attraction to us young kids and those
young nurses. But we were only there three days, and
there were curfews too. You had to be off the streets
at 6:00 p.m., and you couldn't go back onto them until
maybe 6:00 a.m., but that didn't bother us. And we had
to go back to the carrier and eventually left. We
still didn't know what our first target was going to
be. The ACI officer was telling us all about -- well,
one thing we had to learn in the Navy, especially if
you're flying over water and have no place to walk to,
you have to learn all about the weather. And they told
us what kind of clouds to -- all about the different
kind of clouds, and to this day I -- even my wife,
"What kind of a cloud is that? What kind is that?" I
said, "The little ones that look like cotton balls are
called cumulus," but I said, "The ones that are real
high and have a flat top to them, those are anvil
clouds. They're also -- but they're called
cumulonimbus, and you don't want to fly through
there." No pilot, including all today's, would go anywhere near them because that's where the lightning
is and the updrafts. The wind goes up and down. Why,
you'll yo-yo in that thing. That's why there's so many
different sizes of hail. And I flew through a front
one day, and those are usually at a front, and we --
our whole squadron was doing this in formation. And we
kept going up and down because we were trying to find
the ships so we could land. And I can't recall which
one of our missions this was, but I can find out, but
the -- we kept going up and down. They said the
ceiling was 500 feet. We got down to three or 400 and
we still couldn't see the water. So we come back up to
get above the clouds, and we did this for -- several
times, several trips, and finally we did get near the
carriers. And the reason I use the plural is each task
group had four carriers, and at the time we had two
CVLs and two CVs. CV is a -- there again you've got
the Vs. The CV were roughly a thousand feet -- 800
feet, not a thousand, 800 feet. The CVL was about 500
feet. I'm talking flight deck, and that's the only
part we used, so we had to know that. And we flew
through this front not knowing at the time, but when we
got back to the carrier and finally landed, we noticed
that there was no paint on the forward edge of our --
the point that's on the propeller and on the flight --
on the wings, and we knew then that we flew -- went
through something that wasn't friendly. But anyhow, we
survived it. We didn't lose anybody that day, but it
was -- the scary part of it was we kept going up and
down and then we would lose sight of each other, and if
you're flying within a foot or two of another aircraft
and you can't see them, you're careful where you got to
go. You don't want to go into his prop because that
gives you a quick haircut, a permanent one. So we
finally managed to survive all this.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. You flew that close together, though, when --

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Always, except in a bomb -- bombing mission.
We would peel off in our turn, take our turn and do our
bombing. And then when we bombed Iwo Jima and
Okinawa -- this is what I started to say before I hit
the fan -- we had six bombs, and they would only allow
us to drop one at a time. This wasn't area bombing.
This was -- if they -- well, what happened, they had
a -- the Marines on the land would call like another
aircraft and tell them where they needed help. And we
carried a book in our plane of pictures of the entire
island, and they would tell us what sector they were
in, so we would open it up to that sector and then go
look for it. And then they would say what they wanted
bombed in that section. The Navy taught us if we --
when we did -- when we took some of our training, some
in -- I didn't mention this, but Pasco, Washington, was
done after we were all made into a air group and we
were -- we had little bombs about that big that had
a -- like a shotgun shell in it, but it was -- and when
it would hit, it would -- puff of smoke would come up
so we could tell where it hit. And we learned this at
Pasco, Washington, and that's where the -- it wasn't
far from where the nuclear bomb site was, I mean, where
they were making it. We didn't know that either at the
time. And anyway, we would drop these little things,
and we could hit that circle perfectly anytime, so
that's why they sent us and gave me a torpedo plane.
So we would drop one bomb and then go back. If they
needed more bombs in the same area, we would go back
again. In the meantime, we're flying around close
together and get our -- we would get more -- we had to
get rid of all four of our bombs before we went back.
They don't like you flying -- or landing with bombs,
although I did do that once, but fortunately it was
100-pounders and they wouldn't have blown the hell out
of us. Out of me they would have. But I had a
hydraulic problem with the plane. Nothing would open.
The bomb bay wouldn't open. The wheels wouldn't come
down properly. The flaps wouldn't work. I had to do
all this manually, and that was another day that I
probably got a few gray hairs. But anyway, they
finally let me bomb -- or land on the carrier. We were
supposed to -- we were gonna -- what we were gonna do
with these hundred-pounders was drop them on a sled
which one of the battleships had -- we had with us. We
did have the Missouri off and on, but that didn't mean
nothing then. But anyway, we -- I didn't get a chance
to drop mine. I couldn't open the bomb bay, and my
crew were sweating in the back too. But anyway, I
finally got the wheels down, that's the main thing, and
the hook. The hook came down because my crew could
tell me that. And I managed to land safely and didn't
rattle any of the bombs, so I had a good guardian angel
back then. I didn't realize it, but I did later. Kept
me from doing anything foolish.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Those kind of bombs were always armed then?
There was --

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. No, they're not armed until they drop so far.
That's why it's safe to drop and land. But anyway, I
did have a situation on our first flight. That's
another story. But anyway, as I said, we mentioned --
we came all the way over until in January -- or
February 16th I think it was they announced that we
were going to bomb Tokyo. And I said, "You're sending
all us greenhorn ensigns to bomb Tokyo. You don't need
us, do you?" They always told us that we were -- you
know, they had extra ones around. They didn't need us
that bad. But anyway, fortunately the day before we
were going to land there they decided that the weather
was too bad. Guardian angel was at it again. And they
cancelled Tokyo. But then they said Yokohama. I said,
"So what? That's just as bad." We had to fly over
Yokohama to get to Tokyo anyway, so they probably
weren't ________+ -- trouble with Yokohama is they had
ships, and shipping has always got a lot of
antiaircraft guns. I hated to go against shipping.
But anyway, the -- we got to Yokohama. We're all
taking off. We're on the boat together, ready to go.
They called us from the carrier, "We cancelled
Yokohama. You're now going to so-and-so." Nobody can
remember where that so-and-so was. But we started
heading -- this is -- remind me now, this is Japan, not
little islands here and there. But anyway, we're near
the mainland, and we had to let them know we were
getting close. But anyway, we're flying south on the
island of Honshu away from Tokyo, and pretty soon the
skipper of the fighter group comes on the intercom and
says -- told our skipper -- of course, we could talk on
different lines or whatever they want to call them.
Anyway, he called and he says, "We won't make it back
if we go to that mission." So we decided to find our
own. And they found one. They found a little airfield
in the little town of Yazu (ph), I think. I have to
look on my Japanese map, but I -- we didn't know at
the time what it was or where we were. But anyway, we
only luckily had one 2,000-pound bomb that day. They
were giving us that much of a break. They weren't
going to make us do six times -- or four times, so we
dropped it. We found this big hangar, so we
air-conditioned it for them. And there was about five
or six of us, and each one of them dropped their bomb,
and then I was number two. Skipper was number one.
And he goes out and we're rendezvousing, and he finds a
little old boat out in the water, a small one. But he
calls the fighter group and said, "There's a little
boat out here. I want you guys to come and get it and
strafe it," you know, shoot it up or whatever, whatever
they said. But I never heard this conversation for --
learned about it later. And the skipper of the fighter
squadron said, "Sorry, we're too busy chasing trains,
strafing planes," and whatever else was in their path,
and they were having a ball. Nobody shooting back at
them that day or us either. So the skipper decides
that we were going to be -- strafe this little whatever
it was. And so I was number two. I armed my
.50 calibers. First time I ever -- in fact, the only
time I ever used them. And it's -- people say, "Do you
like to fly?" I said, "Not the way they make me fly."
I like to fly low and skim. That's what we did that
day, and I was down to about 50 feet strafing this
little boat. Well, just as I flew over it, the little
bugger blew up. It scared the hell out of me and
knocked the windows out of -- the kind that slide back
and forth, not the front one. That's bulletproof. You
don't blow them out. But anyway, I lost the windows
that protect me from the air, that's all. Plus on the
Avenger there are windows all the way back. They were
all gone. I still don't know to this day what the heck
that ship was, but I think it may have been a mine
layer, and we must have hit one of them. But anyway, I
finished it. It didn't lay any more mines. I must
have hit one of them. So they called me and said, "Are
you okay?" I says, "Yes, I'm fine. I just don't have
any windows." So in the meantime this -- now,
remember, this was in February of 1945, and Tokyo has
the same kind of weather we do in Ohio. So we flew
back to the carrier, and I'm freezing my buns in that
cockpit, and they didn't -- I didn't have to fly too
close going home. We just flew nearby. And I'm flying
home, trying to sit on my hands and fly and this way
and finally got back to the ship, and they said,
"Willert, you're going to land first." I says, "No,
let me fly and land in my regular" -- fly -- "Land
now." So I had to get to the end of the landing
pattern, and then in the carriers when you get into a
landing pattern. You start flying up the starboard
side of the ship and then go all the way up in front
and then come back down and then come in one at a
time. And every 30 seconds you can land a plane
________+ right. But anyway, that day when I came in I
was so damn cold I didn't realize that I was crabbing,
flying sideways, so I hit the deck fine, but the left
wheel went over the side. And then I jumped out
quickly, looked for my crew. They were gone. I said,
"Don't tell me they jumped and didn't tell me." Well,
they hadn't jumped. I found this out a lot later. But
anyway, I delayed all of the landing from then on for
maybe an hour or so, and these guys didn't have a lot
of gas, and that's another thing that bothered you.
But anyway, I went down to the ready room, and they
said, "Where did you bomb?" And I was so cold my
finger must have covered 500 square miles, so they
said, "Willert, get out of here. Go lay down." But
first they gave me a doubleheader. That's the only
time you get a drink in the Navy aboard ship is -- in
fact, we had to bring our own aboard, and the flight
surgeon was in charge of them. So he gave me a
doubleheader. Well, I don't normally drink booze like
that, but I took it anyway. I needed to be warmed up.
So I just sat around, and finally the guys got in all
safely, and then they all decided where we were and
what we had done and -- but I was so ________ cold I
didn't even pay any attention ________. They gave me
another doubleheader when all of the guys were -- I
ended up with three of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. And that's enough to knock me for a loop. So I
went back to my sack, and I fell asleep just like I do
with the television. But we decided that we bombed
Yazu (ph). And after that they didn't bother us so
much. But, in fact, I think the whole -- that thing
will tell you, but I think we headed south after we had
done the first -- this was the first Navy air carrier
bombing of Japan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. I hesitate to ask, but what did happen to
your -- the rest of your crew?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Nothing. They ran like hell to get the hell
off the deck.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. They got out before you came?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Well, they thought that I was going overboard
which --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. -- I don't blame them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. So they managed to --

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. They probably didn't wait until I stopped
rolling because there's a little hold in the side of
the ship of the plane on the right-hand side --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Right.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. -- that you can open up and get in it, and
there's only one guy can get out at a time, but they
both got out. They had to watch the tail, but they got
out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. But they were already down below before you --

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Apparently. I don't know. I really -- I
couldn't see them. I kept asking the boy, I said, "Do
you see my crew?" "No, no." The ship gang wasn't
looking at that. They were watching me. So anyway,
they were -- they were safe. They didn't get hurt,
and then the explosion didn't bother them either. But
my plane did look like hell after I got through. Well,
the wing -- the windows. That's all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. You started to talk about a mission in
South China Sea against ships.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Yes. Well, that was later on, but anyway, they called -- they called our air group. Incidentally, the
task group 58 or 38 are the same thing, but there's
four sections to each task group, 58.1, .2, .3 and .4.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Each task group has four carriers in it. That
means we had 16, a minimum of 16 carriers in a group,
and they're different ones. Sometimes they were
interchangeable, but we were always in number one, our
carrier was.

div2.note: END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE. BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. It was our turn to -- we had torpedoes, our
group -- our plane -- our ship, so they loaded us with
torpedoes that day and told us where to go. Now, every
Navy pilot has a big plastic board that slides into
the -- a slot in the cockpit. Prior to takeoff you'd
had to do your navigation. We didn't have navigators
like the Army did. We had to do everything ourself.
We're the pilot. We're the bombardier. We're the
front gunner and the navigator and the bombardier,
whatever. So we were told to go to the South China Sea
what -- they didn't say that, but they gave us latitude
and longitude. And on this plastic board we would put
down where the fleet was when we took off and where
they're going to be when we come back after so many
hours, and then we would make our -- we had to do this
navigation in the ready room on the ship prior to
takeoff. And we would -- if you ever watch movies,
you'll see every pilot -- I don't know about fighters,
but I think they had to do it too. But they would
carry this big board into the cockpit with them, and
they would slide it in or lock it in, and they wouldn't
look at it until they took -- landed and got out. But
anyway, that one day when we were told from Yokohama
from -- was cancelled -- matter of fact, I think when
we took off, they cancelled Tokyo and then did
Yokohama. We had to -- we had to do our navigation in
the air, and that's a trick. It's hard to fly and
write and all this crap. We didn't do a good job
obviously, but anyway, this -- we went to the
South China Sea and they -- we had a group of about
four cargo ships and a couple of, I think, destroyers.
I'm not too sure, but I didn't see them all. But
anyway, we were -- we were giving -- being allotted to
sink the cargo ships. So I was number two going in on
that too, and we -- I could drop my -- the torpedoes
were good then. I didn't have to go to 50 feet. I
went down to maybe 500 and dropped it, and I blew this
one cargo ship in half. Good shot. What the hell.
That's what I'm trained for. And when we left there
there was nothing floating but debris. All of those
cargo ships and the Navy destroyer, whatever they were,
were gone. They were all sunk. We cleaned that out.
It was at least eight ships. So we cleaned that out
and headed back. That was our first good victory
from -- at least that I -- something that I did because
most of the time I was bombing -- making holes in the
ground, didn't know what the heck I was doing. We
________ bombed some Jap islands that were -- the main
island is called Honshu. The big -- then there was
another one called Kyushu. Incidentally, the -- that
flag up there has got another story too. We were
bombing Okinawa one day and the skipper says, "We're
going to land and wait until the bombing area is
clear. It's clouded now, overcast." We couldn't help
the Marines any, so we landed on an airline -- airfield
call Kadina. Have you heard that lately?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Huh-uh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. That's where that sergeant is from that's being
hit for being raped -- or raping someone.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Okay.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Anyway, this is -- Kadina is one of the most
notable landing strips on that island. And the Marines
took that first, and that's where we -- the Marines had
their home base there. So we landed, and another day
while -- I had four or 500 pounds that day, and I
landed carefully. And my gunner calls me, and he could
see what I'm doing, but he says, "Hey, Pappy" -- and
that's -- that's a new one to me, but we got along that
way. He says, "When you gonna land?" I said, "Mack,
we've been on the ground for three minutes." I landed
very carefully on those 500 -- even though they won't
explode until they -- they have to go through the air
so many feet before they -- they're -- in fact, I did
drop one one day, a 1,000-pounder that never did harm.
It just splattered. I might have squashed a Jap, but I
don't know. But you have to have so many feet before
these things bomb.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Is that like an arming wire, the wire --

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Well, when you release it, the arming process
takes effect. But it has to go so long, and if you're
too damn low, it ain't going to explode.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. So we were careful. The big -- probably
dropped it at 500 feet.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. So he didn't know you had landed, this guy?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Well, he couldn't tell because I landed
carefully that day. And it's -- I said, "Well, Mack,
we're on the ground." So anyway, we taxied to where we
were going to park the planes and turned them off, the
engines, and wandered around, met a few of the Marines,
and the -- one of the Marines had a _______ Jap flag,
and I said, "Hey, you got a spare?" and he says,
"Yeah." "How much?" "20 bucks." I said, "I will
take it." I don't know if I had 20 bucks with me at
the time, but I must have. So I bought it. That was
white. That was clear white and red in the middle.
That was another story. My mother had a -- they had a
smoke fire at my house in Cleveland Heights, and that's
how it got brown. I took it -- I took it back. I was
real proud to get one of those suckers. I took it
back, and I had every ship's officer sign it plus the
air group officers, but you can hardly read them now.
But anyway, they -- I got that for 20 bucks, and when I
brought it home, I had it in a drawer, but it didn't
save it. I had it framed because I wanted to keep it
for posterity, and my youngest son wants it now.
Incidentally, when we were going to -- you can keep
that. I just copied that on the computer this
morning. But anyway, when we were told about Tokyo,
this was the -- a bombing picture that they gave us and
they told us not to bomb here. That's the emperor's
palace.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Right.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. And they didn't want us to get him irritated
because they had a lot of our prisoners over there, and they figured if we'd have killed their emperor, we
would have been in trouble, the whole world would. But
anyway --

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. No, no, that's a copy of a picture.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Oh. Good copy.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Well, nowadays you get better things. And this
is a little history of Air Group 30. Well, after the
torpedo incident, there's an atoll down there in the
Caroline Islands called Ulithi, and it's not far from
Yap, if you ever heard of Yap. Incidentally, Yap is --
was taken over by the Japs at the time, but it's some
kind of a tourist trap now. But anyway, Yap was within
300 miles or whatever. Ulithi is a big
horseshoe-shaped atoll that the U.S. Navy had taken
over, and there were several little islands in a
horseshoe shape. And apparently the coral connected
all of these islands in this horseshoe so that the
entire United States fleet could park in there. So
that means it had to be a big area. At any rate, they
would take us down there about every two weeks. That
was an R and R section, and there was one island where
they removed all of the natives and the Navy took it
over, and first thing the Navy does when they take over
an island is put up a bar, one for the officers, one for the enlisted men. We are allowed three cans of
beer, no more, no less, and then they hand you those
three cans and they open them right away. But some
guys got tricky, but anyway, they would take them back
to the ship. I never did. I would drink them. And on
the lee side of the island were two mountains about the
height of this house of beer cans, empty beer cans, and
there was two of them. And another thing I tell all
the women now, I said, "That was the biggest nude beach
in the world ever and all it was was men, Navy boys."
And I said, "95 percent of them didn't have bathing
suits." Who the hell would have taken a bathing suit
aboard ship going to war? Who needs it? I never even
thought about it. But anyway, I swam there one day,
and I did -- well, I -- of course, when I went to the
island, I had clothes, but I had to remove them to go
swimming. But anyway, I happened to be -- I used to be
a shell-looker-for, you know, find shells. And I
spotted this one little -- it was a nice shell. And I
picked it up, and a little hermit crab was hanging out,
and he reached out and bit my finger. And I dropped it
real quick, and I picked it up and I said, "You son of
a gun." I said, "I was just looking at you. I wasn't
going to eat you." But anyway, I got my lighter out
and I heated the bottom and he popped out. I said, "Now go find another shell. I'm keeping this one."
So I found a bunch of shells, and eventually aboard
ship I -- I was making a necklace and a ring and a
bracelet and just something to kill time aboard ship.
I had other hobbies aboard ship too. And, in fact, I
would go to the ship's dentist, and he gave me some
broken tools, and I would use them. Still got it.
That's -- that was a broken tool. So he gave it to me,
and I -- and then he gave me some cotton and some
plaster of paris, and somehow I got some wire. And I
would curl both ends of the wire, put a slice in the
shell, shove it down with these tools, put some cotton
in it and then some plaster of paris, and that's how I
held them together and I made a necklace. I even used
a dime for a ring, but I don't know where that is
anymore. Anyhow, I got the necklace. Never gave it to
anybody.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Did you have anybody back home that you were
writing to or --

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Oh, did I get letters. I had two cousins and
an aunt at one house, and each one of them wrote
letters separately. I had a girl friend on the West
Coast, which I don't even know where she is anymore.
But, see, we changed bases frequently, and I don't
remember how many of them I did get, but my mother
wrote to me, my aunt and my cousins. I know of one
time -- see, we only get mail about every two weeks,
and I think one of the mail trips I ended up with 23
letters, and I had to write that many. And there
was -- I had all kinds of stationery with me, so I took
that aboard assuming I was going to do a lot of writing
which I did. If I -- my three cousins -- or two
cousins and aunt, if I got a letter from each one of
them on one trip, each one got an answer. I haven't
seen those -- my aunt has passed on, but I still
haven't seen my cousins. One of them lives in Huron,
another one lives in Oleria, so I haven't seen them. I
don't recall who all I wrote to anymore, but I got
plenty of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. What kinds of things did you write about, could
you write about?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Yeah. Well, once in a while I would just tell
them that we're out in the South Pacific, and I would
tell them about Mogmog.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Mogmog?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Yeah, that's the name of the island in Ulithi
that we were allowed to go ashore and had that beach
and the beer cans, and we would sit around there and
shoot the breeze and tell war stories. And I learned
about my former roommate that was taking off one day
with a load of depth charges because he was on a --
what they called anti-sub patrol. And he would --
anti-sub patrol for the Navy, one carrier would be
designated to do it, not every day, but whenever it was
necessary. And you would fly for maybe four hours, and
you would fly a set pattern. The fleet would be going
this way, so if you're -- there was four planes doing
this. One would go up in the front and then back, and
one would be in the back on starboard side and one on
the port side. It was four guys, and you would fly
this program. Every once in a while I would fly over
one of our own cannons, and I had been -- I can recall
looking down five-inch barrels, but I'm only -- I'm at
2,500 feet. We flew low, but that's relatively low.
Anyway, the -- I've looked down five-inch guns. But we
had signals each day, and this particular day we
could -- you drop your right wing twice, and the radio
man in the back had a blinker, and he would give a
signal with his -- with the blinker. I said, "Be sure
you get these guys because they're aiming at us now."
Because our five-inch guns -- a five-inch gun is like
listening to fireworks when those big explosions go
off. Of course, I've never heard one except when I was
aboard the carrier. But the five-inch gun in the Navy
at the time had what they call a proximity fuse in it,
and if it got anywhere near metal, it would explode.
And, of course, if it gets near my plane, it's going to
know it's time to blow. Luckily I've been -- I got
away with it several times, but we would fly this
anti-sub patrol for, as I said, four hours and then
come back to the carrier eventually. Depth charges are
no problem when you land with them because they don't
go off until they're 50 feet or whatever they're set
for. And the reason this story brought -- came up is
when I went to Mogmog, I learned that the guy that was
my roommate was on the San Jacinto and I was on the
Belleau Wood. And I did something wrong back in Frisco
that got me aboard a different ship. I still think it
was my guardian angel that made me do it wrong. But
anyway, he went to the San Jacinto. Incidentally,
President Ford was on that one.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. San Jacinto?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Yeah. And -- or, no, was it Monterey? Anyway,
I think he was on that one. Anyhow, he took off one
day on this anti-sub patrol with the depth charges, and
the skipper of that ship was in a big hurry. He sent
them off before they were into the wind, so when he
took off, he apparently -- or the San Jacinto did not
have catapults, either that or -- whatever happened, he
went into the drink. And his plane got down to where
the depth charges were set for and they blew up, so him
and his crew were killed. And that's what I learned on
Mogmog. Luckily my skipper was never in a big hurry.
But we did have two catapults, even though it was a
smaller ship. Having been hit by this kamikaze in
October, it was home in Frisco being repaired, and they
put two catapults on there. And a catapult really
sends you off. You don't dive down. A lot of them you
see will go down, but an Avenger with the flaps with
that wide -- at least two feet wide and maybe 12 feet
long and one on each side plus the wingspan, so it's a
good plane to take off and land. We had no trouble
landing, and very seldom did I bounce. I always landed
and caught the second or third wire.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. There were three wires across then, is that
right?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. Oh, no, seven or eight.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Nowadays there's probably only three because
they give -- they have -- they're coming in in jets.
They're probably traveling faster than I could fly.
Now I could land the -- probably the ground speed would
be around 70 miles per hour. They're going 150 or
200. And, as I said, our normal speed was around 225
or something, but we didn't do that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. It wasn't -- for you anyway it wasn't that hard
to land it on the carrier?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. No, no, that was very easy. I think it was the
best plane in the world ever to land on a carrier. It
was -- well, I don't know how they were prior to my --
other aircraft, because it just -- it was an excellent
plane for everything, everything. The only problem
they ever had with the torpedo plane was the torpedoes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Unfortunately the torpedo -- the Torpedo
Squadron 8 did not have Avengers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Do you remember any other tough landings other
than that one where you almost went off the side there?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. No, no. All the rest were --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. All were pretty easy?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. -- easy. I made about 26 landings. The record
is up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. About 26 missions?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Yeah, something like that. Like the day I --
when I landed at Kadina, later on that day after I
dropped my bombs, my plane didn't feel right. It
didn't sound right. And I'm still that way today. I
can tell if something's wrong or -- anyhow, I told the
skipper. He says, "Well, land at Kadina and have the
Marines check it." So I did. I landed all by myself.
Nobody else stopped with me. And I let them figure out
the plane. They looked it over. Nothing wrong with
that. Okay. So I had to fly back to the carrier. By
the time I got there, my ship was secure for the day.
In layman's terms, it was closed. No more landings
because they had all the planes for tomorrow already on
the deck where I would have landed. So I had to land
on another carrier, and I think it was the Bennington,
which is a CV. A CVL is a 75-foot-wide landing deck.
The Avenger was 54 1/2 feet wingspan, leaving me about
ten feet on each side. We were aboard -- the Navy only
kept their air groups aboard ship for six months, and
then they would send them home for a leave and then
call them back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. And I was sent home in June of '45 right after
a typhoon knocked the daylights out of our fleet.
Well, it happened to be around Okinawa at the time. We
even lost some of them. Anyway, the -- two of the
carriers in our group -- our task group, the Bennington
and the Hornet, had 25 feet of their flight deck folded
down like somebody just -- like a playing card, and
that -- that really tells you the strength of the
storm. Our carrier didn't do anything, didn't do
anything. It just got tossed about like a cake of
soap. And there are rumors that we almost took water
down the stack, so that meant we were rolling back and
forth. And I will never forget that damn time. That's
12 hours we put up with this, and it started about 2:00
or 2:30 a.m. because one of the folding chairs in our
stateroom -- there's four pilots left in the
stateroom. One of the folding chairs started sliding
back and forth. And the room wasn't much larger than
the one we're in, two bunks over there, two bunks over
here, the hatch to come in, plus we each had a little
hutch which was our own desk and our own safe. But
anyway, I was top bunk on the starboard side and damn
chair started -- woke me up. I said, "What the heck's
going on?" So I got up, got dressed, went down to the
ready room. That's where we always go. That's where
we're supposed to have breakfast or any other meal for
that matter. And I sat down in a ready room chair,
which is about twice the size of the chair you're
sitting on and about four times as heavy. But it's
kind of like a -- one of these fancy chairs they give
us seniors nowadays that you can lean back on, but it
had a little table on it so that we could do our
navigation and what have you. And they were down in
the officer's mess. That's where our ready room was.
So I went down there and sat in this chair, and pretty
soon -- somehow or the other, the only thing holding it
to the steel deck was a little angled piece of metal
that kept it where it was. Well, that broke loose. So
I sit on this damn ready room chair all by myself, and
the ship is going over from one side to the other, and
I'm riding back and forth on this in the ready room,
and I'm having a ball. I thought, "Gee, this is a good
ride." And we'd hit the damn wall on one side and come
back and hit something else, and there were a number of
tables in there which were kind of like -- had sleeves
in them, and it would hit the table and the table would
get shorter. So finally I thought, "This could be
dangerous," so I got out of the chair and jumped up on
one of these tables. And then the chair continued to
knock leaves out while I'm laying on it. Nobody else
is doing this, just me. And no breakfast available,
not even a hard-boiled egg. I think one of them did
roll by, but I don't know who got it. But anyway, I
finally got -- got off the table and I waited until I
had a chance, and I ran toward the exit, which was a
little screen door, and it was locked. I says, "Why
would this be locked? How are we going to get out of
here?" And I found out later some ship's officer whose
brain was in his underwear locked it. Why I don't
know, but he was also nosy and he wanted to see how
high the waves were, so he opens the hatch and lets in
a wave of water. So we had water sloshing all over
that area, and this idiot from the ship of all people
that should have known better.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Anyway, I finally got out, and I just sat
around and waited until it subsided. Then I went down
to the flight -- the hangar deck. All of our planes
were put down there because they knew this was coming.
They don't have local Dopplers like they got now, nor
did they have planes looking at the top of one of these
storms to see which way it's going. But Bull Halsey,
seemed like every time he took over the fleet, it was
his turn to get a typhoon. His first typhoon he got
stuck for three days. The second one luckily was only
a half a day. He got smarter. So we -- we finally got
out of this typhoon because we had a leave and headed
in an opposite direction. In the meantime, we lost
about five or six destroyers that were actually sunk
because of it. Here's a picture of the Hornet, what it
did to it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Whoa.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. We were -- we were all sitting on a flight on
the hangar deck one night. The whole fleet was parked
in this atoll, and we were watching a movie. Suddenly
all the lights went out. General quarters blows.
Well, they didn't even bother with that, but they just
turned the lights out, and, I mean, that was like
standing in a closet with no light within 50 feet. It
was black, and they -- "You're on your own now. Go
back to your whatever," wherever you could go that you
could have some light because it -- we found out later
that a Jap aircraft from the island of Yap flew over
the atoll and dive-bombed or kamikazed one of the
islands thinking it was a carrier. So he made a
failure out of himself. But that's what the lights
went out for.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Of course, they didn't know it at the time.
And that was another thing that I kind of remembered
because I had to find my way in the dark with
absolutely no lights whatsoever. I don't know how I
did it yet, but I found my way out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Got back to the ready room or wherever -- I
don't even remember where, but we survived that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. So you said you were watching a movie.
Anything else you did for entertainment over there?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Oh, we used to play Solitaire and Acey-Deucey
and I don't know what all. Most of the time we were
shooting the breeze with each other and telling tales
of whatever. Well, if we weren't on a flight, it was
boring, believe me. But then when we found out they
were coming back, why, we would try to watch, if we
could. There were occasions where at night you would
go up to -- on the flight deck and just stand there.
And one night suddenly GQ is sounded again, general
quarters, and the kamikazes were coming. Of course, we
didn't know from where. But when you've got a
battleship, two or three cruisers, four carriers and I
don't know how many cannons all shooting up in the air,
you have really seen fireworks. And I will never see
fireworks like that here in the States. But I watched
the fireworks. And one night we were noticing one of
our destroyers was firing and his tracers -- these were
all tracers -- were getting lower and lower, and I
said, "Let's get the heck off of this deck." And we
went over to the side, and pretty soon that stopped.
And I was supply officer for my squadron, and the next
day I had one of those little rides where you go from
one ship to another on the boatswain's chair they call
it. Well, I floated over to this other cannon, and
they were going to take me to another carrier so I
could pick something up, probably another plane.
Anyhow, the -- we were talking to the skipper of the
cannon who was probably a captain or whatever, and we
were telling him -- I said, The other night while we
were watching all those fireworks, one of the ship's
tracers were almost over our deck," and he said, "Don't
tell anybody, but that was us." He says, "Our radar
picked you guys up, and it just automatically takes the
guns with it." So he said they have to overreact and
cut that off, cease fire. So that was the end of that
one. We did have other things that happened that are
recallable, but they're not -- once in a while I
would -- I would take -- I was the only one that did
this type of work for the squadron. I would go to
another carrier and pick up a plane or just some
supplies and then come back, do the same thing again.
The one pilot that died last October was on -- we were
on our shakedown cruise where we were learning how to
land on a Jeep carrier, and he -- and he was -- I did
mine. I think we made about six or eight landings. He
was doing his, and he was one of the earlier ones. And
he's taking off. I think I was watching, and suddenly
he starts to slow down and his plane goes right over
the bow into the water. Well, we found out later on
that he -- he thought he was going too slow, so he was
going to put on the brakes, and you don't do that when
you're in an Avenger, but anyway, he went over the
side. And he got out, and he was picked up by a
cannon, and he stayed on the cannon for a while and
played cards with the skipper and beat him out of some
money. Found out later he had -- we used to call him
Wild Bill Mosey (ph). He had completely demolished
three Avengers and never got a scratch. And he's the
one that we just lost last October or November, one of
my closest buddies. So that's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Did they have any U.S.O. shows or anything that
you saw ________+?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Oh, I went to those when I was in Indiana.
Matter of fact, that's when we were flying the
Stearman.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. I did go to the U.S.O. And there was one young
lady there that kind of -- I liked to see her and talk
to her and dance with her and all that stuff, and I
found out where she lived. I got in my Stearman one
day, and I says, "I know where she lives now." I don't
know how I did this, but I think I looked in the phone
book, found out her last name. So I looked and found
out where the farm was, and I was probably 1,500 feet
or so, and I cut the engine and coasted down. And just as I got to the farmyard I gunned the engine, and it
roars when you do that. And I think there were
chickens and horses and cows flying in the air that
day, but I got the heck out of here before they saw my
number. I found out about later, she says, "Oh, they
do that all the time in our neighborhood." Didn't
bother them apparently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. You came home in June of '45 then, right?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. When your tour was up?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Actually I was -- no. I was on my way home in
June. I think by the time I got out of Frisco it was
July already. And I was home on leave when they
dropped the biggies, and, of course, I was -- my
original orders were to return to San Francisco and
perhaps go back, well, aboard another carrier. I don't
know which one or how. But the war ended while I was
home on leave, and I was still living in the Cleveland
Heights area with my parents. And one of my neighbors
up there was -- well -- well, the girl was a high
school friend. She had a convertible, and anytime I
came home they would let me have that convertible. So
we were -- I was sitting in the back -- I don't know if
I was driving or not. But anyway, the night the war
ended -- well, everybody was celebrating, but it was
dark, and we were riding up and down Euclid Avenue, and
it started to rain. And we were in this convertible,
and it would rain and then it would stop and then it
would rain and stop, so we kept taking the top down.
It was automatic, so we'd open it up and then we would
close it. I don't think I was driving, but I did have
my Navy uniform on, and I kept my hat on so in case any
other car went by they would know it was a serviceman
because back in those days you could ride free on the
streetcars and buses if you had a uniform on, so I took
advantage of all that. But I was home on leave, and I
got new orders, report to Jacksonville, Florida, naval
air base or what have you. So I get down there. They
gave me three choices, get in, get out or stay in or
something like that. So I says, "I'll go out." And
then I went downtown and got my pilot's license or --
not that it was going to do me any good. I didn't have
any multi-engine plane time anyway. But anyhow, I got
the license while we were there, and we were there a
month before we finally got out. I had to make up
about -- oh, about, eight or ten hours of flying
time. So we end up in these slow-moving aircraft to
fly around doing nothing, just fly from point A to B
and back and forth, and after three or four hours we'd
come down. In the Navy you had to get a minimum of
four hours per month in order to get flight pay, and
flight pay was 50 percent of your base pay. An ensign
gets $200 a month back in those days. And I would fly
the -- well, of course, I didn't need to worry about
flight pay overseas, but I would get my four hours in
and I'd -- I got 300 a month. And they also -- the
Navy charges their officers back in those days -- I
don't know what it is now -- a dollar a day for food.
They don't charge you for a meal. They charge you a
dollar a day for food no matter where you're at. So --
and that's deducted. And I didn't spend a lot of
money, so I made other arrangements to buy bonds. I
bought a bunch of war bonds or whatever they called
them back then, and even aboard ship I think all I got
was like 20 or 30 bucks a month. There's nothing to
buy on board ship other than cigarettes, and a carton
of cigarettes back in those days was 55 cents. The tax
on one pack is more than that now. So I'd buy a carton
of cigarettes, and that would last me a couple of
months because I didn't smoke much. And there were
certain places the smoking lamp is out and you -- if
they were transferring oil or fuel or whatever from one
ship to another, you don't smoke. That's --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Most of your missions were then against -- like
on Iwo Jima, did you go in soon after that was invaded?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Actually my ________ went there, but I ended up
doing this anti-sub patrol because that Iwo Jima
mustn't have been more than a week for us, and we don't
take off every day. It's -- when you've got four
carriers in a task group, each carrier gets the job for
whatever it is.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. And I think all I did at Iwo personally was fly
anti-sub patrol. But I have, which I will show you, if
I can find them, a book of Iwo Jima pictures so we knew
where to bomb.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Uh-huh, right.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. And being supply officer for the squadron, I
ended up with these things because I turned things in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Right. So you ________+?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. I brought my flight jacket home too, and I
even -- I brought my -- some other junk that I -- I
never brought any guns home or binoculars. Primarily
what I did leave the ship with was a whole flock of
cigarettes. I must have had about ten cartons, and our
suitcases back in those days were soft, not hard box
like they do now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Did you ever hit a sub when you were out there
________+?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Never found one. Never even saw one. Never
even saw a Jap.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Scared them away. Never saw a Jap?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Well, by the time I got up there, we were in
control.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Right.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. And that was fortunate. And I always blame or
give the credit to my angel --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. -- for keeping me out of harm's way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Did you have the same thing about Okinawa too?

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Oki, yeah. We had the books, but I apparently
turned my back because I don't have one of those,
but -- because I dropped a total of 49 bombs on
Okinawa, and only twice I think were they more than
500. It's no fun to drop -- make one run. We enjoyed
this, but what I mentioned before when I spilled the
beans, I was starting to say that I didn't like the
system that the Navy had. Even though I had to go down
four times on a mission, they only counted it one.
Now, to my mind, that would have been four because I
got shot at four times, not once. And, well, you'll
see over there on my missions, but Okinawa was kind of
like a milk run. We were bombing it -- D Day on
Okinawa was April 1st of 1945, and that was not only
Easter Sunday, but it was -- they called it Love Day.
That was the -- and it would be L minus ten, you would
be doing this and so on now. So we did that. We
bombed Okinawa before the Marines and the Army. The
Marines were at the north end and the Army was at the
southern end. Now, the Marines went through the north
in a day or two, but there was not too much opposition,
although they are wilder than most. The Army boys
weren't trained the same way. And anyway, as I
mentioned, they were -- when we finally got over there
and had these pictures taken so we'd know where to
bomb, we could drop that 500-pound right nearby
________. And it was -- it got to be a pretty easy
deal. Some places -- see, Okinawa, when you're
bombing -- as I mentioned before, I don't like bombing
ships, and occasionally on some other little islands
we'd go down -- these ships had a hell of a lot of fire
power. We learned that the hard way. My skipper was
hit and right in front of me and he went in. I didn't
see it because my plane is in the way, and I dropped my
bombs and got the heck out of there. And I think that
day I dropped them all at once because we were trying
to -- I don't even know what I hit because the skipper
was hurt that day -- or killed. We didn't -- I
didn't -- I was more involved with that than I was --
and boys -- the rest of the crew joined up on me
thinking I was the skipper.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Right.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. I found out later that his crew jumped. He
went down with the plane, but the crew jumped -- maybe
he did too, but the crewmen from other planes saw that
the Japs machine-gunned them while they were in the
air. That's why we hate things -- that's why I hate
things in Japanese, made in Japan. Even when I see a
Toyota now, I don't like it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Sorry.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p: A. Is that what you got out there?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. You're not the first one that was in my yard.
My daughter in Columbus had a Honda, same feeling.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Right.

sp.speaker: William Willert
sp.p:
A. Made there. It was designed there. In fact,
last night we saw one and and my wife said, "That's a
nice looking car." The first thing that came to mind,
they're the best copiers in the world.
